questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.topic: Diagnosis of pregnancy, antenatal imaging & fetal surveillance
questions.stem: The earliest and most accurate ultrasound parameter for dating a pregnancy is:
options: Crown-rump length in the first trimester
questions.concept: Crown-rump length between 7 and 13 weeks dates pregnancy to within 5 to 7 days because early embryonic growth is remarkably uniform. Accuracy falls progressively later as biological variation increases.

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.topic: Diagnosis of pregnancy, antenatal imaging & fetal surveillance
questions.stem: A non-stress test is described as reactive when there are:
options: Two or more accelerations of 15 beats for 15 seconds in 20 minutes
A baseline of 100 beats per minute
questions.concept: A reactive trace shows at least two accelerations of 15 beats per minute lasting 15 seconds within 20 minutes, with a baseline of 110 to 160 and good variability, indicating an intact fetal autonomic nervous system and absence of acidosis.

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.topic: Diagnosis of pregnancy, antenatal imaging & fetal surveillance
questions.stem: Which fetal heart rate pattern is most ominous?
options: Recurrent late decelerations with absent variability
questions.concept: Late decelerations beginning after the contraction peak reflect uteroplacental insufficiency, and when combined with absent variability indicate fetal acidaemia requiring prompt delivery. Early decelerations from head compression are benign.

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.topic: Diagnosis of pregnancy, antenatal imaging & fetal surveillance
questions.stem: The components of the biophysical profile include all EXCEPT:
questions.concept: The biophysical profile scores fetal breathing, gross body movement, tone, amniotic fluid volume and the non-stress test, each out of 2 for a maximum of 10. Estimated fetal weight is not a component.

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.topic: Diagnosis of pregnancy, antenatal imaging & fetal surveillance
questions.stem: Absent or reversed end-diastolic flow in the umbilical artery on Doppler indicates:
options: Severe placental insufficiency requiring urgent delivery consideration
questions.concept: Rising placental vascular resistance first reduces, then abolishes and finally reverses end-diastolic flow, marking critical fetal compromise. Ductus venosus a-wave reversal is the last change before decompensation.

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.topic: Diagnosis of pregnancy, antenatal imaging & fetal surveillance
questions.stem: Nuchal translucency for aneuploidy screening is measured between:
questions.concept: Nuchal translucency is measured at a crown-rump length of 45 to 84 mm, combined with maternal age, free beta-hCG and PAPP-A in the first trimester combined test. Increased translucency suggests trisomy 21, 18, 13 or cardiac defects.

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.topic: Diagnosis of pregnancy, antenatal imaging & fetal surveillance
questions.stem: Maternal serum alpha-fetoprotein is characteristically raised in:
questions.concept: Raised AFP occurs with open neural tube defects, abdominal wall defects, multiple pregnancy and wrong dates, whereas low AFP with low unconjugated oestriol and raised hCG suggests trisomy 21 on the triple test.

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.topic: Diagnosis of pregnancy, antenatal imaging & fetal surveillance
questions.stem: Chorionic villus sampling is performed at which gestation, and carries what principal added risk over amniocentesis?
options: 10 to 13 weeks, with a higher fetal loss rate and limb reduction if done before 10 weeks
16 to 18 weeks with no added risk
20 weeks with risk of preterm labour
At term with risk of bleeding
questions.concept: CVS is done at 10 to 13 weeks giving earlier results than amniocentesis at 15 to 18 weeks, but carries slightly higher pregnancy loss and, if performed before 10 weeks, limb reduction defects and oromandibular hypogenesis.

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.topic: Diagnosis of pregnancy, antenatal imaging & fetal surveillance
questions.stem: Cell-free fetal DNA testing in maternal blood is best described as:
options: A highly sensitive screening test that requires confirmation by invasive testing
A test for neural tube defects
questions.concept: Non-invasive prenatal testing analyses placental cell-free DNA from about 10 weeks with very high detection for trisomy 21, but a positive result is a screen positive and must be confirmed by karyotyping of amniotic fluid or villi.

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.topic: Diagnosis of pregnancy, antenatal imaging & fetal surveillance
questions.stem: Quickening, the first maternal perception of fetal movement, occurs in a primigravida at about:
questions.concept: A primigravida perceives movement at 18 to 20 weeks and a multigravida about two weeks earlier at 16 to 18 weeks, as she recognises the sensation sooner. It is a soft clinical marker of gestational age.

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.topic: Medical disorders in pregnancy: anaemia, diabetes, heart disease
questions.stem: Anaemia in pregnancy as per WHO is defined as haemoglobin below:
questions.concept: WHO defines anaemia in pregnancy as haemoglobin below 11 g/dL; the Indian national programme grades 10 to 10.9 as mild, 7 to 9.9 as moderate, below 7 as severe and below 4 g/dL as very severe or decompensated.

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.topic: Medical disorders in pregnancy: anaemia, diabetes, heart disease
questions.stem: Parenteral iron in pregnancy is indicated when:
options: Oral iron is not tolerated or absorbed, or anaemia is moderate with insufficient time before delivery
questions.concept: Intravenous iron sucrose or ferric carboxymaltose is used for intolerance or failure of oral iron, malabsorption, or moderate anaemia after the first trimester when there is too little time to correct by mouth. Blood transfusion is reserved for severe decompensated anaemia near term.

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.topic: Medical disorders in pregnancy: anaemia, diabetes, heart disease
questions.stem: Screening for gestational diabetes with the DIPSI single-step 75 g oral glucose test is positive when the 2-hour value is:
questions.concept: The Indian DIPSI approach gives 75 g glucose irrespective of fasting status and diagnoses gestational diabetes at a 2-hour value of 140 mg/dL or above, chosen for feasibility in community settings.

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.topic: Medical disorders in pregnancy: anaemia, diabetes, heart disease
questions.stem: The commonest fetal complication of poorly controlled gestational diabetes is:
questions.concept: Fetal hyperinsulinaemia from maternal hyperglycaemia drives macrosomia with the risk of shoulder dystocia and birth trauma, along with neonatal hypoglycaemia, hypocalcaemia, polycythaemia and respiratory distress. Pre-gestational diabetes additionally causes congenital malformations.

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.topic: Medical disorders in pregnancy: anaemia, diabetes, heart disease
questions.stem: The oral hypoglycaemic agent most accepted in pregnancy when insulin is refused is:
options: Glibenclamide only in the first trimester
questions.concept: Insulin remains the standard, but metformin is increasingly accepted, does not cause maternal hypoglycaemia and crosses the placenta without evidence of teratogenicity. Thiazolidinediones and gliptins are avoided.

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.topic: Medical disorders in pregnancy: anaemia, diabetes, heart disease
questions.stem: The most dangerous cardiac lesion in pregnancy is:
questions.concept: Pulmonary hypertension carries maternal mortality of 30 to 50% because the fixed pulmonary vascular resistance cannot accommodate the increased cardiac output, and pregnancy is contraindicated. Eisenmenger physiology worsens with the fall in systemic resistance.

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.topic: Medical disorders in pregnancy: anaemia, diabetes, heart disease
questions.stem: In a pregnant woman with rheumatic mitral stenosis, the period of greatest haemodynamic risk is:
options: The second stage of labour and immediate postpartum period
questions.concept: Cardiac output peaks in late second stage and immediately after delivery when uterine autotransfusion adds 500 mL to the circulation, precipitating pulmonary oedema. Second stage is therefore shortened with assisted delivery and epidural analgesia.

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.topic: Medical disorders in pregnancy: anaemia, diabetes, heart disease
questions.stem: Anticoagulation of choice in a pregnant woman with a mechanical heart valve is:
options: Low molecular weight heparin, or warfarin only in the second trimester by specialist decision
questions.concept: Warfarin is teratogenic in the first trimester and causes fetal intracranial bleeding near term, so heparin is preferred; heparin does not cross the placenta. Direct oral anticoagulants are contraindicated in pregnancy.

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.topic: Medical disorders in pregnancy: anaemia, diabetes, heart disease
questions.stem: Peripartum cardiomyopathy is defined as new-onset heart failure occurring:
options: In the last month of pregnancy or within five months of delivery with no other cause
At any time in a woman with prior heart disease
questions.concept: Peripartum cardiomyopathy presents with left ventricular systolic dysfunction in the last month of pregnancy or up to five months postpartum in the absence of another cause, and recurs in subsequent pregnancies, especially if ejection fraction does not normalise.

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.topic: Medical disorders in pregnancy: anaemia, diabetes, heart disease
questions.stem: Antiepileptic drug most associated with neural tube defects when used in pregnancy is:
questions.concept: Valproate carries the highest risk of neural tube defects and neurodevelopmental impairment and is avoided in women of childbearing age. Levetiracetam and lamotrigine are preferred, with 5 mg folic acid periconceptionally.

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.topic: Infections in pregnancy & Rh isoimmunisation
questions.stem: Anti-D immunoglobulin is given to an Rh-negative mother:
options: Within 72 hours of delivery of an Rh-positive baby and after any sensitising event
Only if the baby is Rh negative
questions.concept: Anti-D 300 micrograms is given within 72 hours of delivery of an Rh-positive infant, and after abortion, ectopic pregnancy, amniocentesis, external cephalic version or antepartum haemorrhage; routine antenatal prophylaxis is given at 28 weeks.

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.topic: Infections in pregnancy & Rh isoimmunisation
questions.stem: The most sensitive non-invasive test to detect fetal anaemia in Rh isoimmunisation is:
options: Middle cerebral artery peak systolic velocity on Doppler
questions.concept: Anaemia lowers blood viscosity and raises cardiac output, increasing middle cerebral artery peak systolic velocity above 1.5 multiples of the median. It has replaced serial amniocentesis for bilirubin (Liley curve) in surveillance.

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.topic: Infections in pregnancy & Rh isoimmunisation
questions.stem: The Kleihauer-Betke test is used to:
options: Quantify fetomaternal haemorrhage to calculate the anti-D dose
questions.concept: The acid-elution Kleihauer test counts fetal cells resistant to acid in the maternal circulation, quantifying fetomaternal haemorrhage so additional anti-D can be given when the bleed exceeds 15 mL of fetal red cells.

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.topic: Infections in pregnancy & Rh isoimmunisation
questions.stem: The classical triad of congenital rubella syndrome is:
options: Limb defects, cleft palate and anaemia
questions.concept: Congenital rubella causes cataract, patent ductus arteriosus or pulmonary artery stenosis and sensorineural deafness, with maximum risk in the first trimester. The intracranial calcification triad belongs to toxoplasmosis.

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.topic: Infections in pregnancy & Rh isoimmunisation
questions.stem: The commonest congenital infection worldwide, and leading infectious cause of sensorineural deafness, is:
questions.concept: Congenital CMV affects about 0.5 to 1% of births, causing periventricular calcification, microcephaly, chorioretinitis, hepatosplenomegaly and blueberry-muffin rash, and is the leading infectious cause of sensorineural hearing loss.

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.topic: Infections in pregnancy & Rh isoimmunisation
questions.stem: To prevent mother-to-child transmission of HIV, the current recommendation is:
options: Lifelong maternal antiretroviral therapy with infant prophylaxis and exclusive feeding of one type
questions.concept: Lifelong maternal ART reduces transmission to below 2%, with infant nevirapine prophylaxis and exclusive breastfeeding or exclusive replacement feeding, never mixed feeding. Vaginal delivery is acceptable when the viral load is suppressed.

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.topic: Infections in pregnancy & Rh isoimmunisation
questions.stem: Congenital syphilis is best prevented by:
options: Screening with VDRL at the first antenatal visit and treating with benzathine penicillin
questions.concept: Universal VDRL or RPR screening at booking with benzathine penicillin treatment prevents almost all congenital syphilis; penicillin is the only adequate drug and penicillin-allergic women are desensitised rather than given alternatives.

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.topic: Infections in pregnancy & Rh isoimmunisation
questions.stem: Primary varicella infection in pregnancy carries greatest risk of congenital varicella syndrome when acquired:
questions.concept: Congenital varicella syndrome - limb hypoplasia, cicatricial skin scarring, chorioretinitis and cortical atrophy - is greatest between 8 and 20 weeks. Maternal infection within 5 days before to 2 days after delivery risks severe neonatal varicella and needs VZIG.

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.topic: Infections in pregnancy & Rh isoimmunisation
questions.stem: Hepatitis E in pregnancy is important because it:
options: Causes fulminant hepatic failure with mortality up to 20 percent in the third trimester
questions.concept: Hepatitis E has a markedly increased case fatality in the third trimester with fulminant hepatic failure, obstetric haemorrhage and high fetal loss. Prevention is through safe drinking water as no vaccine is widely available in India.

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.topic: Infections in pregnancy & Rh isoimmunisation
questions.stem: Asymptomatic bacteriuria in pregnancy must be treated because untreated it leads to:
options: Pyelonephritis, preterm labour and low birth weight
questions.concept: Up to 30% of untreated asymptomatic bacteriuria progresses to acute pyelonephritis in pregnancy with preterm labour and low birth weight, so all pregnant women are screened by urine culture and treated.

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.topic: Abnormal labour: malpresentation, obstructed labour, CPD
questions.stem: The commonest type of breech presentation is:
questions.concept: Frank breech with hips flexed and knees extended accounts for about 60 to 70% and has the lowest risk of cord prolapse. Footling breech carries the highest risk and is a contraindication to vaginal delivery.

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.topic: Abnormal labour: malpresentation, obstructed labour, CPD
questions.stem: External cephalic version for breech presentation is usually attempted at:
options: 36 to 37 weeks in a nulliparous woman
questions.concept: Version is offered at 36 to 37 weeks in nulliparas and from 37 weeks in multiparas, when spontaneous version is unlikely but delivery can follow if complications arise. Contraindications include placenta praevia, ruptured membranes and prior classical caesarean.

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.topic: Abnormal labour: malpresentation, obstructed labour, CPD
questions.stem: Bandl's ring in obstructed labour represents:
options: A pathological retraction ring at the junction of upper and lower uterine segments
questions.concept: Persistent obstruction causes progressive retraction of the upper segment, producing a visible transverse groove across the abdomen - Bandl's ring - with a distended lower segment and impending rupture. It is an obstetric emergency.

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.topic: Abnormal labour: malpresentation, obstructed labour, CPD
questions.stem: The commonest cause of obstructed labour in India is:
questions.concept: Cephalopelvic disproportion, often from a contracted pelvis in a short or malnourished woman, is the leading cause, followed by malpresentation and malposition such as deep transverse arrest and brow presentation.

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.topic: Abnormal labour: malpresentation, obstructed labour, CPD
questions.stem: Which presentation is absolutely incompatible with vaginal delivery at term in a living fetus?
options: Brow presentation with a persistent mento-vertical diameter
questions.concept: Brow presentation presents the mento-vertical diameter of about 13.5 cm, the largest, and cannot deliver vaginally unless it converts to face or vertex. Mento-anterior face presentation can deliver vaginally.

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.topic: Abnormal labour: malpresentation, obstructed labour, CPD
questions.stem: Shoulder dystocia is initially managed by:
options: Strong downward traction on the head
questions.concept: McRoberts hyperflexion of the maternal hips with suprapubic pressure resolves most cases. Fundal pressure is contraindicated as it worsens impaction, and excessive traction causes brachial plexus injury.

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.topic: Abnormal labour: malpresentation, obstructed labour, CPD
questions.stem: The commonest cause of a prolonged second stage in a nullipara is:
questions.concept: Persistent occipito-posterior position presents a larger diameter and causes deflexion, prolonged labour with early backache and a strong urge to push before full dilatation. Most rotate spontaneously to occipito-anterior.

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.topic: Abnormal labour: malpresentation, obstructed labour, CPD
questions.stem: A partogram crossing the action line indicates:
questions.concept: The WHO partogram plots cervical dilatation against time with alert and action lines; crossing the alert line prompts transfer to a facility, and crossing the action line requires assessment and intervention such as augmentation or caesarean.

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.topic: Abnormal labour: malpresentation, obstructed labour, CPD
questions.stem: The most reliable clinical sign of obstructed labour with impending rupture is:
options: Maternal tachycardia with a tender uterus, haematuria and cessation of contractions after a Bandl ring
questions.concept: Established obstruction produces maternal exhaustion and dehydration, a tender continuously contracting uterus with a Bandl ring, haematuria from bladder compression, and then sudden cessation of pain with shock when rupture occurs.

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.topic: Abnormal labour: malpresentation, obstructed labour, CPD
questions.stem: Symphysiotomy or destructive operations are now largely replaced by:
questions.concept: With safe anaesthesia and blood availability, caesarean section has replaced destructive procedures such as craniotomy and decapitation, which are now reserved for a dead fetus in obstructed labour where caesarean is unavailable.
